Content:
A standard vibrating system under an external force [MATH: f(t)] looks like
[MATH: y'' + \omega^2y = f(t),]
where [MATH: \omega] is the system's natural internal frequency.

Content:
The complementary solution [MATH: y_c] describes the system's internal oscillation when there is no external force. It can be written as
[MATH: y_c = A\cos(\omega t) + B\sin(\omega t),]
so the motion naturally oscillates at frequency [MATH: \omega.]

Content:
If the external force [MATH: f(t)] is periodic, then it has its own forcing frequency [MATH: \omega_e.] Resonance occurs when the forcing frequency matches the natural frequency:
[MATH: \omega_e = \omega]

Content:
Intuitively, resonance happens because the force repeatedly "pushes" the system at exactly the right rhythm each cycle. In the undamped model, these pushes add energy coherently over time, so the amplitude of the oscillations increases without bound.

Content:
For example, suppose the position [MATH: y(t),] measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with periodically forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation
[MATH: y'' + 36y = -6\cos^2{pt},]
where [MATH: t>0] is the time, in seconds. Let's find the value of the parameter [MATH: p] that causes the oscillator to resonate.

Content:
Notice that the complementary solution has frequency [MATH: \omega,] where [MATH: \omega^2=36.] Therefore,
[MATH: \omega=6.]

Content:
The external force is
[MATH: f(t)=-6\cos^2{pt} = -3(1+2\cos{2pt}),]
which has forcing frequency [MATH: \omega_e=2p.]

Content:
Resonance occurs when [MATH: \omega_e=\omega,] so
[MATH: p=\dfrac{\omega}{2} = 3.]

items.title: Calculating the Value of a Parameter that Results in Resonance

sections.normalized_html:
The position [MATH: y(t),] measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with periodically forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

[MATH: y'' + 25y =2\sin^2{pt},]

where [MATH: t > 0] is the time, in seconds. Which value of the parameter [MATH: p] causes the oscillator to resonate?
sections.readable_text:
The position [MATH: y(t),] measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with periodically forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

[MATH: y'' + 25y =2\sin^2{pt},]

where [MATH: t > 0] is the time, in seconds. Which value of the parameter [MATH: p] causes the oscillator to resonate?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find the general solution of the differential equation. The complementary solution [MATH: y_c] here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

[MATH: y_c=A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t}.]

In our case,

[MATH: \omega^2 = 25\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \omega = 5,]

so, we have

[MATH: y_c=A\cos{5 t} + B\sin{5 t}.]

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force [MATH: 2 \sin^2 pt] is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution, which is [MATH: \omega = 5.] Since

[MATH: f(t) = 2 \sin^2 pt = 1 - \cos 2pt,]

the frequency of the external periodic force is [MATH: 2p.] Therefore, the oscillator experiences resonance when [MATH: 2p = 5 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p = \dfrac{5}{2}.]

items.title: Determining the Spring Constant Given an External Periodic Force

sections.normalized_html:
A particle of mass [MATH: 0.25\,\textrm{kg}] is attached to a massless spring. An external periodic force [MATH: F(t) = 3\sin(6t)\,\textrm{N}] is applied to the particle.

The position of the particle is [MATH: y(t)] (measured in meters), and [MATH: t>0] is the time in seconds. If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion without damping and the system experiences resonance, what is the spring constant [MATH: k?]
sections.readable_text:
A particle of mass [MATH: 0.25\,\textrm{kg}] is attached to a massless spring. An external periodic force [MATH: F(t) = 3\sin(6t)\,\textrm{N}] is applied to the particle.

The position of the particle is [MATH: y(t)] (measured in meters), and [MATH: t>0] is the time in seconds. If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion without damping and the system experiences resonance, what is the spring constant [MATH: k?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The equation of motion for a particle of mass [MATH: m] moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant [MATH: k] and external force [MATH: F(t)] is given by

[MATH: my'' = -ky + F(t).]

Substituting our values for [MATH: m] and [MATH: F(t)] gives

[MATH: 0.25y'' = - ky + 3\sin(6t).]

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

[MATH: y'' + 4ky = 12\sin(6t).]

The complementary solution [MATH: y_c] here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

[MATH: y_c = A\cos \omega t + B\sin \omega t,]

where [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are arbitrary constants of integration, and [MATH: \omega] is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

[MATH: \omega^2 = 4k \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad k = \dfrac14\omega^2.]

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force [MATH: f(t)=12\sin(6t),] which is [MATH: 6,] is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution [MATH: \omega.]

Therefore, [MATH: k = \dfrac14\omega^2 = \dfrac14\cdot6^2 = 9 \,\textrm{kg/s}^2.]

items.title: General Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations With Resonance

sections.normalized_html: Consider an undamped forced oscillator, [MATH: y''+\omega^2y=f(t),] where [MATH: \omega] is the system's natural frequency. Its general solution is [MATH: y=y_c+y_p,] where [MATH: y_c] solves the homogeneous equation [MATH: y''+\omega^2y=0] and [MATH: y_p] is any particular solution to the full equation.
sections.readable_text:
Consider an undamped forced oscillator,
[MATH: y''+\omega^2y=f(t),]
where [MATH: \omega] is the system's natural frequency. Its general solution is
[MATH: y=y_c+y_p,]
where [MATH: y_c] solves the homogeneous equation [MATH: y''+\omega^2y=0] and [MATH: y_p] is any particular solution to the full equation.

sections.normalized_html: Notice that the complementary solution can be written in any of the following equivalent forms:
sections.readable_text: Notice that the complementary solution can be written in any of the following equivalent forms:

sections.normalized_html:
1. [MATH: y_c = R\cos{(\omega t + \phi_1)}]

  2. [MATH: y_c = R\sin{(\omega t + \phi_2)}]

  3. [MATH: y_c =A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t}]
sections.readable_text:
1. [MATH: y_c = R\cos{(\omega t + \phi_1)}]
2. [MATH: y_c = R\sin{(\omega t + \phi_2)}]
3. [MATH: y_c =A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t}]

sections.normalized_html: Now, suppose the external force has the resonant form [MATH: f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),] so that the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency [MATH: \omega.]
sections.readable_text:

[MATH: f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),]
so that the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency [MATH: \omega.]

sections.normalized_html: A sinusoidal trial at frequency [MATH: \omega] would duplicate [MATH: y_c,] so at resonance we multiply by [MATH: t] and use a trial of the form [MATH: y_p=t\bigl(C\cos(\omega t)+D\sin(\omega t)\bigr).]
sections.readable_text:
A sinusoidal trial at frequency [MATH: \omega] would duplicate [MATH: y_c,] so at resonance we multiply by [MATH: t] and use a trial of the form
[MATH: y_p=t\bigl(C\cos(\omega t)+D\sin(\omega t)\bigr).]

sections.normalized_html: To determine [MATH: C] and [MATH: D,] we first compute derivatives: [MATH: y_{p}^{′}|= C\cos (ωt) + D\sin (ωt) + t(− Cω\sin (ωt) + Dω\cos (ωt)); y_{p}^{″}|= 2(− Cω\sin (ωt) + Dω\cos (ωt)) − tω^{2}(C\cos (ωt) + D\sin (ωt))]

To determine [MATH: C] and [MATH: D,] we first compute derivatives:
[MATH: y_{p}^{′}|= C\cos (ωt) + D\sin (ωt) + t(− Cω\sin (ωt) + Dω\cos (ωt)); y_{p}^{″}|= 2(− Cω\sin (ωt) + Dω\cos (ωt)) − tω^{2}(C\cos (ωt) + D\sin (ωt))]

sections.normalized_html: Substituting into the equation, we have that the [MATH: t]-terms cancel out, and we obtain [MATH: y_{p}^{″} + ω^{2}y_{p} = 2ωD\cos (ωt) − 2ωC\sin (ωt).]
sections.readable_text:
Substituting into the equation, we have that the [MATH: t]-terms cancel out, and we obtain
[MATH: y_{p}^{″} + ω^{2}y_{p} = 2ωD\cos (ωt) − 2ωC\sin (ωt).]

sections.normalized_html: Since we need [MATH: y_p''+\omega^2y_p=f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),] equating coefficients gives [MATH: 2\omega D=a, \qquad -2\omega C=b.]

Since we need [MATH: y_p''+\omega^2y_p=f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),] equating coefficients gives
[MATH: 2\omega D=a,
\qquad
-2\omega C=b.]

sections.normalized_html: Therefore, [MATH: C=-\frac{b}{2\omega}, \qquad D=\frac{a}{2\omega},] so a standard resonant particular solution is [MATH: y_p =\frac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr).]

Therefore,
[MATH: C=-\frac{b}{2\omega},
\qquad
D=\frac{a}{2\omega},]
so a standard resonant particular solution is
[MATH: y_p =\frac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr).]

[MATH: y_{p}^{′}|= C\cos (ωt) + D\sin (ωt) + t(− Cω\sin (ωt) + Dω\cos (ωt)); y_{p}^{″}|= 2(− Cω\sin (ωt) + Dω\cos (ωt)) − tω^{2}(C\cos (ωt) + D\sin (ωt))]

Content:
Substituting into the equation, we have that the [MATH: t]-terms cancel out, and we obtain
[MATH: y_{p}^{″} + ω^{2}y_{p} = 2ωD\cos (ωt) − 2ωC\sin (ωt).]

Content:
Since we need [MATH: y_p''+\omega^2y_p=f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),] equating coefficients gives
[MATH: 2\omega D=a,
\qquad
-2\omega C=b.]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: C=-\frac{b}{2\omega},
\qquad
D=\frac{a}{2\omega},]
so a standard resonant particular solution is
[MATH: y_p =\frac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr).]

Content:
So, when [MATH: f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t)] and resonance occurs, the general solution can be written as
[MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y=A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)+\dfrac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr)}.]

3. [MATH: y = A\cos(4t) + B\sin(4t) - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t)]

Note that [MATH: A,] [MATH: B,] [MATH: R,] and [MATH: \phi] are constants.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency [MATH: \omega.]

The external force is [MATH: f(t)=4\cos(4t)+12\sin(4t),] which is sinusoidal with frequency [MATH: 4.] Therefore, [MATH: \omega = 4.]

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

  1. [MATH: y_c = R\cos{(\omega t + \phi)} = R\cos{(4t + \phi)}]

  2. [MATH: y_c = R\sin{(\omega t + \phi)} = R\sin{(4t + \phi)}]

  3. [MATH: y_c =A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t} = A\cos(4t) + B\sin(4t)]

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency [MATH: \omega] duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by [MATH: t] and take a resonant particular solution of the form [MATH: y_p(t)=t(C\cos(4t)+D\sin(4t)).]

By substituting the particular solution and [MATH: \omega=4] into the differential equation, [MATH: y'' + \omega^2y = f(t),] we get [MATH: [8(D − 2Ct)\cos (4t) − 8(C + 2Dt)\sin (4t)] + 16t(C\cos (4t) + D\sin (4t))|= 4\cos (4t) + 12\sin (4t); 8D\cos (4t) − 8C\sin (4t)|= 4\cos (4t) + 12\sin (4t)]

Equating coefficients, [MATH: C=-\dfrac{3}{2}] and [MATH: D=\dfrac{1}{2}.]

So, the particular solution is [MATH: y_p(t) = -\dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t).]

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

  1. [MATH: y = R\cos{(4t + \phi)} - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t)]

  2. [MATH: y = R\sin{(4t + \phi)} - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t)]

  3. [MATH: y = A\cos(4t) + B\sin(4t) - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t)]

Only solutions I and II match the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

Content:
Recall that resonance is the phenomenon where an external periodic force drives a vibrating system at exactly the system's natural frequency. In the undamped model, this causes the oscillations to grow larger and larger over time.

Content:
In the ideal undamped model, resonance produces a particular solution that grows in magnitude with time (due to the extra factor of [MATH: t]). This is why the model predicts that the amplitude increases without bound.

Content:
For example, consider the undamped forced oscillator
[MATH: y'' + 9y = \sin(3t).]
The complementary solution is of the form [MATH: y_c = A\cos(3t) + B\sin(3t),] the natural frequency of the system is [MATH: \omega = 3,] and the forcing frequency is also [MATH: 3.] Because these frequencies match, resonance occurs.

Content:
Since the forcing term [MATH: \sin(3t)] duplicates a term in the homogeneous solution, we must multiply our guess by [MATH: t.] We try a solution of the form [MATH: y_p = t(C\cos(3t) + D\sin(3t)).]

Content:
Calculating the derivatives of [MATH: y_p,] substituting them into the equation, and equating coefficients of [MATH: \sin(3t)] and [MATH: \cos(3t)] yields [MATH: C=-\dfrac16] and [MATH: D=0.] So, the particular solution is of the form
[MATH: y_p = -\dfrac{t}{6}\cos(3t).]
Notice that this solution grows larger as [MATH: t] increases. This time-dependent growth illustrates how resonance leads to an increase in oscillation amplitude in the undamped model.

Content:
In real systems, perfectly unbounded growth does not occur because physical effects, such as damping and energy loss, eventually limit the amplitude. Even so, forcing near the natural frequency can still produce very large oscillations, which is why resonance is important in engineering design.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A standard vibrating system under an external force [MATH: f(t)] looks like
[MATH: y'' + \omega^2y = f(t),]
where [MATH: \omega] is the system's natural internal frequency.

Content:
The complementary solution [MATH: y_c] describes the system's internal oscillation when there is no external force. It can be written as
[MATH: y_c = A\cos(\omega t) + B\sin(\omega t),]
so the motion naturally oscillates at frequency [MATH: \omega.]

Content:
If the external force [MATH: f(t)] is periodic, then it has its own forcing frequency [MATH: \omega_e.] Resonance occurs when the forcing frequency matches the natural frequency:
[MATH: \omega_e = \omega]

Content:
Intuitively, resonance happens because the force repeatedly "pushes" the system at exactly the right rhythm each cycle. In the undamped model, these pushes add energy coherently over time, so the amplitude of the oscillations increases without bound.

Content:
For example, suppose the position [MATH: y(t),] measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with periodically forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation
[MATH: y'' + 36y = -6\cos^2{pt},]
where [MATH: t>0] is the time, in seconds. Let's find the value of the parameter [MATH: p] that causes the oscillator to resonate.

Content:
Notice that the complementary solution has frequency [MATH: \omega,] where [MATH: \omega^2=36.] Therefore,
[MATH: \omega=6.]

Content:
The external force is
[MATH: f(t)=-6\cos^2{pt} = -3(1+2\cos{2pt}),]
which has forcing frequency [MATH: \omega_e=2p.]

Content:
Resonance occurs when [MATH: \omega_e=\omega,] so
[MATH: p=\dfrac{\omega}{2} = 3.]

Content:
Let's see more examples.

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Value of a Parameter that Results in Resonance

Example Prompt:
The position [MATH: y(t),] measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with periodically forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

[MATH: y'' + 25y =2\sin^2{pt},]

where [MATH: t > 0] is the time, in seconds. Which value of the parameter [MATH: p] causes the oscillator to resonate?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we find the general solution of the differential equation. The complementary solution [MATH: y_c] here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

[MATH: y_c=A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t}.]

In our case,

[MATH: \omega^2 = 25\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \omega = 5,]

so, we have

[MATH: y_c=A\cos{5 t} + B\sin{5 t}.]

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force [MATH: 2 \sin^2 pt] is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution, which is [MATH: \omega = 5.] Since

[MATH: f(t) = 2 \sin^2 pt = 1 - \cos 2pt,]

the frequency of the external periodic force is [MATH: 2p.] Therefore, the oscillator experiences resonance when
[MATH: 2p = 5 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p = \dfrac{5}{2}.]

---

Item 5 — Example: Determining the Spring Constant Given an External Periodic Force

Example Prompt:
A particle of mass [MATH: 0.25\,\textrm{kg}] is attached to a massless spring. An external periodic force [MATH: F(t) = 3\sin(6t)\,\textrm{N}] is applied to the particle.

The position of the particle is [MATH: y(t)] (measured in meters), and [MATH: t>0] is the time in seconds. If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion without damping and the system experiences resonance, what is the spring constant [MATH: k?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The equation of motion for a particle of mass [MATH: m] moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant [MATH: k] and external force [MATH: F(t)] is given by

[MATH: my'' = -ky + F(t).]

Substituting our values for [MATH: m] and [MATH: F(t)] gives

[MATH: 0.25y'' = - ky + 3\sin(6t).]

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

[MATH: y'' + 4ky = 12\sin(6t).]

The complementary solution [MATH: y_c] here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

[MATH: y_c = A\cos \omega t + B\sin \omega t,]

where [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are arbitrary constants of integration, and [MATH: \omega] is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

[MATH: \omega^2 = 4k
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
k = \dfrac14\omega^2.]

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force [MATH: f(t)=12\sin(6t),] which is [MATH: 6,] is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution [MATH: \omega.]

Therefore,
[MATH: k = \dfrac14\omega^2 = \dfrac14\cdot6^2 = 9 \,\textrm{kg/s}^2.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: General Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations With Resonance

Content:
Consider an undamped forced oscillator,
[MATH: y''+\omega^2y=f(t),]
where [MATH: \omega] is the system's natural frequency. Its general solution is
[MATH: y=y_c+y_p,]
where [MATH: y_c] solves the homogeneous equation [MATH: y''+\omega^2y=0] and [MATH: y_p] is any particular solution to the full equation.

Content:
Notice that the complementary solution can be written in any of the following equivalent forms:

Content:
1. [MATH: y_c = R\cos{(\omega t + \phi_1)}]
2. [MATH: y_c = R\sin{(\omega t + \phi_2)}]
3. [MATH: y_c =A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t}]

Content:
Now, suppose the external force has the resonant form
[MATH: f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),]
so that the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency [MATH: \omega.]

Content:
A sinusoidal trial at frequency [MATH: \omega] would duplicate [MATH: y_c,] so at resonance we multiply by [MATH: t] and use a trial of the form
[MATH: y_p=t\bigl(C\cos(\omega t)+D\sin(\omega t)\bigr).]

Content:
To determine [MATH: C] and [MATH: D,] we first compute derivatives:
[MATH: y_{p}^{′}|= C\cos (ωt) + D\sin (ωt) + t(− Cω\sin (ωt) + Dω\cos (ωt)); y_{p}^{″}|= 2(− Cω\sin (ωt) + Dω\cos (ωt)) − tω^{2}(C\cos (ωt) + D\sin (ωt))]

Content:
Substituting into the equation, we have that the [MATH: t]-terms cancel out, and we obtain
[MATH: y_{p}^{″} + ω^{2}y_{p} = 2ωD\cos (ωt) − 2ωC\sin (ωt).]

Content:
Since we need [MATH: y_p''+\omega^2y_p=f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t),] equating coefficients gives
[MATH: 2\omega D=a,
\qquad
-2\omega C=b.]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: C=-\frac{b}{2\omega},
\qquad
D=\frac{a}{2\omega},]
so a standard resonant particular solution is
[MATH: y_p =\frac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr).]

Content:
So, when [MATH: f(t)=a\cos(\omega t)+b\sin(\omega t)] and resonance occurs, the general solution can be written as
[MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y=A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)+\dfrac{t}{2\omega}\bigl(-b\cos(\omega t)+a\sin(\omega t)\bigr)}.]

Item 9 — Example: Identifying Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations

Example Prompt:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
[MATH: f(t) = 4\cos(4t)+12\sin(4t).]
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position [MATH: y(t)?]

1. [MATH: y = R\cos(4t+\phi) - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t)]
2. [MATH: y = R\sin(4t+\phi) - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t)]
3. [MATH: y = A\cos(4t) + B\sin(4t) - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t)]

Note that [MATH: A,] [MATH: B,] [MATH: R,] and [MATH: \phi] are constants.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency [MATH: \omega.]

The external force is [MATH: f(t)=4\cos(4t)+12\sin(4t),] which is sinusoidal with frequency [MATH: 4.] Therefore,
[MATH: \omega = 4.]

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1. [MATH: y_c = R\cos{(\omega t + \phi)} = R\cos{(4t + \phi)}]
2. [MATH: y_c = R\sin{(\omega t + \phi)} = R\sin{(4t + \phi)}]
3. [MATH: y_c =A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t} = A\cos(4t) + B\sin(4t)]

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency [MATH: \omega] duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by [MATH: t] and take a resonant particular solution of the form
[MATH: y_p(t)=t(C\cos(4t)+D\sin(4t)).]

By substituting the particular solution and [MATH: \omega=4] into the differential equation, [MATH: y'' + \omega^2y = f(t),] we get
[MATH: [8(D − 2Ct)\cos (4t) − 8(C + 2Dt)\sin (4t)] + 16t(C\cos (4t) + D\sin (4t))|= 4\cos (4t) + 12\sin (4t); 8D\cos (4t) − 8C\sin (4t)|= 4\cos (4t) + 12\sin (4t)]

Equating coefficients, [MATH: C=-\dfrac{3}{2}] and [MATH: D=\dfrac{1}{2}.]

So, the particular solution is
[MATH: y_p(t) = -\dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t).]

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1. [MATH: y = R\cos{(4t + \phi)} - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t)]
2. [MATH: y = R\sin{(4t + \phi)} - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t)]
3. [MATH: y = A\cos(4t) + B\sin(4t) - \dfrac{3}{2}t\cos(4t) + \dfrac{1}{2}t\sin(4t)]

Only solutions I and II match the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

Item 12 — Tutorial: Practical Resonance

Content:
Recall that resonance is the phenomenon where an external periodic force drives a vibrating system at exactly the system's natural frequency. In the undamped model, this causes the oscillations to grow larger and larger over time.

Content:
In the ideal undamped model, resonance produces a particular solution that grows in magnitude with time (due to the extra factor of [MATH: t]). This is why the model predicts that the amplitude increases without bound.

Content:
For example, consider the undamped forced oscillator
[MATH: y'' + 9y = \sin(3t).]
The complementary solution is of the form [MATH: y_c = A\cos(3t) + B\sin(3t),] the natural frequency of the system is [MATH: \omega = 3,] and the forcing frequency is also [MATH: 3.] Because these frequencies match, resonance occurs.

Content:
Since the forcing term [MATH: \sin(3t)] duplicates a term in the homogeneous solution, we must multiply our guess by [MATH: t.] We try a solution of the form [MATH: y_p = t(C\cos(3t) + D\sin(3t)).]

Content:
Calculating the derivatives of [MATH: y_p,] substituting them into the equation, and equating coefficients of [MATH: \sin(3t)] and [MATH: \cos(3t)] yields [MATH: C=-\dfrac16] and [MATH: D=0.] So, the particular solution is of the form
[MATH: y_p = -\dfrac{t}{6}\cos(3t).]
Notice that this solution grows larger as [MATH: t] increases. This time-dependent growth illustrates how resonance leads to an increase in oscillation amplitude in the undamped model.

Content:
In real systems, perfectly unbounded growth does not occur because physical effects, such as damping and energy loss, eventually limit the amplitude. Even so, forcing near the natural frequency can still produce very large oscillations, which is why resonance is important in engineering design.
